awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Eye Movement Patterns as Early Indicators of Alzheimer's Disease
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this I-Corps project is the development of a non-invasive eye-tracking system designed for the early detection of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Current diagnostic methods used to detect AD such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans are expensive and inaccessible for many, particularly in under-resourced areas. The new technology aims to change how AD is diagnosed by enabling healthcare providers to identify cognitive decline at its earliest stages, with the goal of improving patient outcomes. By offering a more affordable and user-friendly solution, this system has the potential to be integrated into routine healthcare settings, making early AD detection more widely available. In addition, this eye-tracking system may meet the growing demand for diagnostic tools in neurology, with applications extending to both clinical and research environments.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of an advanced eye-tracking technology integrated with machine learning algorithms to diagnose Alzheimer’s disease (AD). The technology leverages bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) networks and attention mechanisms, and analyzes subtle changes in eye movement patterns that are indicative of early cognitive decline associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Preliminary research has demonstrated that changes in ocular biomarkers may serve as reliable early indicators of AD, and this system capitalizes on that discovery. Through technical validation, the project has shown promising results in accurately detecting early signs of AD, offering a non-invasive alternative to traditional neuroimaging and cognitive assessments. The technology combines machine learning with practical, real-world applications, offering a solution for early diagnosis in neurodegenerative diseases.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report 

Award Title: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Eye Movement Patterns as Early Indicators of Alzheimer’s Disease
Federal Award ID: 2444897
Report Period: 11/15/2024 – 10/31/2025

This I-Corps project examined whether health-care stakeholders would adopt an eye-movement–based screening approach for earlier recognition of cognitive decline, and what real-world constraints would shape that adoption. The work focused entirely on customer discovery-not on product development-by testing problem, value, workflow, evidence, and purchasing hypotheses with prospective customers and influencers.

Through approximately 125 stakeholder engagements, including in-person visits to local clinics and senior-care centers, nationwide virtual interviews with clinicians, and targeted calls with health-care administrators, the team mapped who feels the pain of late or difficult detection, who would use and champion a new screening approach, and who ultimately pays. These conversations clarified the different roles of primary-care physicians, geriatric specialists, memory-care teams, and nursing staff in screening workflows, as well as the influence of administrators on procurement and integration decisions. 

Interviewees consistently emphasized four adoption drivers: non-invasiveness, speed at the point of care, fit with existing clinical workflows, and affordability relative to imaging and other costly diagnostics. They also highlighted two gating requirements before any pilot: clear clinical validation evidence and straightforward integration with existing documentation systems. From these inputs, the team reframed its initial assumptions from “feature performance” to “workflow compatibility plus evidence,” and shifted messaging from technical novelty to measurable operational benefits such as shorter triage time, earlier referral when appropriate, and the possibility of more equitable access in under-resourced settings.

Customer discovery refined segmentation and early-market focus. General primary-care settings showed interest but expressed concerns about time pressure and competing screening priorities; by contrast, geriatric and memory-care clinics reported stronger enthusiasm given their patient mix and staff familiarity with cognitive assessment. Nurses emerged as key users for administering an initial screener if the process could be completed within a few minutes and documented automatically in the chart. Administrators underscored the centrality of reimbursement clarity, clinical guidelines, and total cost of ownership when evaluating novel screeners.

The project outcome is an evidence-based view of where an eye-movement screener could plausibly fit and what is required to earn adoption. Specifically, the work produced: (1) a refined problem statement centered on access, workflow simplicity, and cost; (2) a value proposition that prioritizes objective, non-invasive triage and longitudinal monitoring; (3) a buyer and champion map spanning clinicians, nursing staff, and administrators; and (4) a validation checklist that includes prospective study design, interoperability with electronic records, and a reimbursement narrative aligned with stakeholder expectations.

By focusing on customers, not construction, this I-Corps effort clarified the real-world conditions under which an eye-movement–based approach could extend early screening options for cognitive decline. The findings will inform any later evidence-generation and partnership decisions outside the scope of I-Corps, with the aim of improving timely access to assessment pathways if future development and validation meet stakeholder requirements.
